question: When an overparameterized denoising-score model can eventually fit the empirical score and reproduce its training set, do its optimization dynamics first pass through a long generalizing regime, how do the generalization and memorization times scale with dataset size and model width, and can a random-feature spectral model explain that separation?

key_findings.claim: The paper starts from the standard observation that exact minimization of empirical denoising score matching learns the score of a Gaussian mixture centered on the training examples and therefore drives reverse diffusion toward training samples.
key_findings.evidence: Equations (3)-(5) distinguish population and empirical score matching and write the empirical noisy density explicitly as an n-component Gaussian mixture. The authors cite prior work for the high-dimensional statement that avoiding sample recreation under this exact empirical score can require n exponential in data dimension.

anchors.section: Setting: generative diffusion and score learning, Eqs. (3)-(5)

key_findings.claim: On grayscale 32-by-32 CelebA with a roughly 4-million-parameter U-Net, sample quality appears early while the nearest-neighbor copying statistic appears later and its onset approximately collapses under training-step rescaling by n.
key_findings.evidence: For n from 512 to 4096, Figure 2 places the FID minimum around 100,000 SGD updates while normalized f_mem curves rise around tau/n approximately 300. At n=1024, the displayed early checkpoint has FID 30.1 and f_mem=0%, whereas the 1.62-million-step checkpoint has FID 19.1 and f_mem=34.1%.

anchors.section: Figure 2 and Role of training set size on the learning dynamics

key_findings.claim: The loss diagnostic supports delayed overfitting rather than only delayed visible copying: train and test denoising losses first coincide, then separate on an n-scaled time, and copying begins after that separation.
key_findings.evidence: At fixed diffusion time t=0.01, Figure 2 shows training loss continuing downward while test loss rises after a dataset-dependent critical time; the inset collapses the curves against tau/n. The authors report that n=32768 still has nearly coincident losses after 11 million updates and note a lag from loss overfitting to f_mem onset.

anchors.section: Figure 2, middle panel and final paragraph

key_findings.claim: A full-batch ablation rules out a simple count-of-repeated-exposures explanation over the small dataset range tested, but it does not by itself establish a unique loss-landscape cause.
key_findings.evidence: With B=n for n between 128 and 512, every example is used once per update, yet the normalized memorization curves still approximately collapse versus tau/n. This rejects equal per-example exposure as a sufficient explanation; the stronger statement that the loss landscape is the cause is an interpretation because gradient dimension, batch size, stochasticity, and dataset geometry all change with n.

anchors.section: Memorization is not due to data repetition
A.2 Batch-size effect: repetition vs. memorization

key_findings.claim: Changing U-Net base width produces the reported scalings tau_gen proportional to W^-1 and tau_mem proportional to n/W; this is a width law, not a demonstrated inverse law in the literal trainable-parameter count p.
key_findings.evidence: Widths W in {8,16,32,48,64} correspond to p in {0.26,1,4,9,16} million, approximately p proportional to W squared. Figure 3 collapses FID against tau W and copying against tau W/n, so the same evidence is closer to tau proportional to p^-1/2 across this architecture family.

anchors.section: Figure 3 and Effect of the model capacity

key_findings.claim: The displayed U-Net phase boundaries are finite-training empirical contours, while the architectural threshold n-star(p) at infinite training is extrapolated rather than observed.
key_findings.evidence: Figure 3 measures the minimum n with f_mem(tau)=0 at tau_gen, 3 tau_gen, and 8 tau_gen. The text says the curves are expected to converge as tau tends to infinity and estimates n-star(p) from an apparent plateau at a practical tau_max of 2 million updates; no infinite-time limit or uncertainty on that extrapolation is supplied.

anchors.section: Figure 3, right panel and final paragraph

key_findings.claim: The natural-image evidence is deliberately controlled but narrow: one unconditional, downsampled, grayscale face dataset, no augmentation, 18 distinct model configurations, and one training realization per configuration is described.
key_findings.evidence: The supplement specifies center-cropped 32-by-32 grayscale CelebA, n=128 to 32768, no augmentation, 1M-16M-parameter U-Nets, and 18 models. FID uncertainty comes from five disjoint test sets and loss uncertainty from repeated noise evaluations; the manuscript does not report independent retraining seeds for the CelebA scaling curves.

anchors.section: A.1 Dataset, Architecture, Training, and Generation
A.1 Statistical evaluation and Computing resources

key_findings.claim: The reported uncertainty does not quantify run-to-run optimization variability, so the precision of the scaling exponents is weaker than the plotted confidence bands may suggest.
key_findings.evidence: FID error bars use different held-out test subsets, train/test-loss bars use noise re-evaluations, and f_mem uses bootstrap resampling of generated samples. All reuse a trained model and therefore omit initialization, data-subset, and SGD-trajectory variance; the supplement gives no slope regression or confidence interval for the claimed exponent one in n.

key_findings.claim: The memorization endpoint is metric-dependent and measures close pixel-space replicas, not all forms of training-data memorization.
key_findings.evidence: Equation (6) calls a sample memorized when the expected ratio of squared L2 distance to its first and second nearest training neighbors is below k=1/3. Sensitivity checks use k=1/2 and 1/4, but the test can miss semantic, partial, transformed, or distributional memorization; FID can simultaneously improve while exact-copy fraction rises.

key_findings.claim: Adam and conditional-generation checks are positive scope extensions, but each is a small fixed-hyperparameter demonstration rather than a general optimizer or conditioning law.
key_findings.evidence: A W=64 U-Net run with Adam at learning rate 1e-4 shows the same qualitative two-stage pattern and approximate tau_mem proportional to n. Conditional evidence is a classifier-free-guided d=8 two-component Gaussian mixture at W=64 and n in {256,512,1024}; the paper explicitly leaves absolute dependence on the conditioning variable open.

anchors.section: B.3 Discussion on conditional diffusion models

key_findings.claim: A synthetic Gaussian-mixture experiment reproduces an n/W-delayed degradation using a directly estimable population target, though the width dependence of the generalization time remains inconclusive.
key_findings.evidence: For a d=8 balanced two-Gaussian mixture and a roughly 102K-parameter residual MLP, Figure 9 shows KL divergence first approaching zero and then rising with f_mem. Curves collapse approximately under tau/n and tau W, while Section B.2 explicitly says the dependence of tau_gen on W is unresolved.

anchors.section: B.2 Scaling of tau_mem and tau_gen with n and W, Figure 9

key_findings.claim: The random-feature analysis makes the optimization time constants exactly spectral within its model: gradient flow is linear in the learned second-layer matrix and relaxes along eigenmodes of the empirical feature correlation U.
key_findings.evidence: The score is a frozen-first-layer random-feature network, the second layer is initialized at zero, and score matching is performed at one fixed diffusion time. Equation (10) gives linear gradient flow, Proposition C.1 solves it in closed form, and the relaxation factors contain exp(-2 Delta_t U tau/psi_p).

anchors.section: 3 Training dynamics of a Random Features Network, Eqs. (7)-(11)
C.2 Closed form of the learning dynamics, Proposition C.1

key_findings.claim: In the strongly overparameterized asymptotic random-feature regime, the paper identifies a fast population-covariance bulk and a slow finite-sample bulk, yielding tau_gen of order 1/Delta_t and tau_mem of order psi_n/Delta_t.
key_findings.evidence: Theorem 3.2 decomposes the spectrum into an irrelevant atom plus rho_1 on scale psi_p/psi_n and rho_2 on scale psi_p when psi_p is much larger than psi_n. Because training time is inverse eigenvalue after the Delta_t/psi_p rescaling, the two bulks generate an n-independent fast stage and an n-linear slow stage; Figure 5 shows loss curves collapsing under the predicted slow time.

anchors.section: Figure 5 and Emergence of the two timescales during training

key_findings.claim: The random-feature symbol p counts frozen features, whereas the learned matrix A contains d times p parameters; identifying its n-star=p transition with a generic sample-versus-trainable-parameter phase boundary is therefore only qualitative.
key_findings.evidence: Equation (7) defines W in R^{p by d} as frozen and A in R^{d by p} as learned. The asymptotic ratios are psi_p=p/d and psi_n=n/d, and Section 3 states n-star(p)=p in this feature-count sense. The U-Net plots instead label p as total trainable parameters, so the horizontal axes do not share the same operational definition.

key_findings.claim: The theoretical bridge to practical diffusion training is limited by fixed-noise, frozen-feature, high-dimensional, and initialization assumptions.
key_findings.evidence: The theory trains a separate score at a single diffusion time t, assumes p,n,d tend jointly to infinity, bounded-spectrum sub-Gaussian data, a Hermite-expandable activation, zero-mean activation, and A(0)=0. Practical U-Nets condition one model over all noise times and use learned convolutional/attention features with SGD momentum or Adam.

key_findings.claim: The manuscript is internally inconsistent about rigor for the general-covariance spectral result.
key_findings.evidence: The proof preamble says the replica-method section is non-rigorous but the final result is rigorous because it can alternatively be obtained from the free-random-matrix approach of prior work. Two pages later, the generalized Gaussian-equivalence derivation for arbitrary covariance says that following the rigorous route is left for future work. Theorem 3.2 is also explicitly labeled informal and its first-bulk ansatz is said to be checked numerically.

anchors.section: C Proofs of the analytical results, opening paragraph

key_findings.claim: Some proof steps silently specialize beyond the stated sub-Gaussian-data assumptions, further weakening the claim of a fully general covariance theorem.
key_findings.evidence: The Gaussian-equivalence discussion invokes central-limit and entrywise O(1/n) arguments without an operator-norm error bound. In Lemma C.5 the proof writes X as Sigma^{1/2} Z with standard Gaussian entries when bounding sample covariance, which is exact for Gaussian elliptical data but not for an arbitrary sub-Gaussian distribution having covariance Sigma.

key_findings.claim: The intermediate random-feature score error decreases empirically with dataset ratio, but its displayed exponent is a fitted observation rather than a theorem.
key_findings.evidence: Figure 13 fits E_score-star approximately 0.20 psi_n^-0.59 across the tested points. Section D states that an accurate estimate of the exponent and a theory for it are left to future work; the KL bound also requires integrating score error across all diffusion times, whereas the plotted experiment is at one t.

anchors.section: D Scaling of E_score with n, Eqs. (218)-(219)

key_findings.claim: Spectral and optimizer supplements are consistency checks rather than independent tests of the full generative claim.
key_findings.evidence: Figures 11-15 vary fixed diffusion time, data variance, finite-size spectra, and Adam for Gaussian random features. They verify curve collapse and spectral histograms under the model assumptions, but do not sample a full all-t reverse diffusion process or evaluate image originality in that model.

anchors.section: D Effect of t and Scaling of E_score

key_findings.claim: The paper's broad extension to flow matching and other score-based generators is a mechanism-level conjecture, not evaluated evidence.
key_findings.evidence: The conclusion says the score-learning mechanism is common to stochastic interpolants and flow matching and therefore is expected to generalize. All reported image experiments are DDPM/DDIM, while the synthetic experiments remain diffusion score models.

key_findings.claim: The strongest headline result has near-complete concurrent overlap with Bigger Isn't Always Memorizing, which was publicly submitted one day earlier and is acknowledged by the authors only after completion.
key_findings.evidence: The present paper's page 11 acknowledgment names Favero, Sclocchi, and Wyart as independently studying the same transition. Exact-version review of arXiv:2505.16959v2 shows the same central empirical law tau_mem proportional to dataset size, a pre-memorization generalization window, and an early-stopping phase diagram across image and language diffusion; the present paper's clearest distinct contribution is its random-feature spectral account plus width, full-batch, Adam, and Gaussian-mixture ablations.

anchors.section: Related works and stated training-time novelty

method.core_idea: Track a diffusion score network throughout optimization rather than only at convergence, define a sample-quality time tau_gen and a copying/overfitting time tau_mem, measure how both change with dataset size and network width, and explain their separation through fast and slow eigenvalue bulks in a solvable random-feature score model.
method.mechanism: The empirical score contains a smooth population-like component and a dataset-specific irregular component, especially at low noise. Gradient-based networks learn the smoother component first, producing useful novel samples, while much longer training is needed to resolve the finite-sample component and reproduce examples. In the random-feature model, a population-covariance spectral bulk relaxes on an O(1/Delta_t) scale and a finite-sample bulk relaxes on an O(n/delta_t d) scale, making early stopping an implicit dynamical regularizer.
assumptions: The nearest-neighbor ratio in downsampled pixel L2 is an adequate operational measure of training-example memorization.
A visually identified FID minimum and copying onset define stable tau_gen and tau_mem across configurations.
Training-step count is the relevant time variable even when optimizer, batch size, width, and per-step compute differ.
The observed n-linear collapse over the finite n range extrapolates beyond the tested points and stochastic training runs.
For U-Net phase diagrams, base width W is a useful one-dimensional proxy for expressivity and total parameter count.
The finite two-million-step plateau is informative about an infinite-training architectural threshold.
The random-feature mechanism at one fixed diffusion time transfers to a learned U-Net conditioned across all diffusion times.

The random-feature asymptotic uses d,p,n to infinity with fixed ratios, a Hermite-expandable activation, sub-Gaussian data with bounded covariance spectrum, zero activation mean, and zero second-layer initialization.
The Gaussian-equivalence and replica calculations capture the spectrum sufficiently despite acknowledged non-rigorous steps for general covariance.
Fast and slow spectral components of a frozen-feature model are representative of spectral bias in trained deep convolutional score networks.

techniques.role: Measures sample quality, train/test score loss, and nearest-neighbor copying at many checkpoints instead of evaluating only a converged diffusion model.
Rescales optimization steps by n to test the empirical law tau_mem proportional to n.
Rescales steps by U-Net width W and n/W to estimate generalization and memorization time dependence on model capacity.
Declares a generated image memorized when its first-to-second training-neighbor squared-distance ratio falls below a fixed threshold.
Keeps per-example exposure per update equal across small n to test whether delayed copying is merely caused by less repetition.
Solves frozen-feature score-matching gradient flow and maps its relaxation times to eigenvalue bulks of the empirical feature correlation matrix.
Approximates nonlinear random features by a Gaussian covariate model and derives Stieltjes-transform equations for general covariance.
Uses a known two-Gaussian population score to measure KL degradation and copying under dataset, width, and conditioning interventions.

evaluations.setting: Unconditional DDPM U-Nets on grayscale 32-by-32 CelebA, W=32, n from 512 to 4096, with 10,000 generated samples per checkpoint
evaluations.metric: FID to 10,000 test images and nearest-neighbor memorization fraction f_mem
evaluations.result: FID reaches its minimum around 100K updates across n; normalized f_mem rises around tau/n approximately 300. For n=1024, the displayed 100K checkpoint has FID 30.1 and 0% memorization, versus FID 19.1 and 34.1% at 1.62M updates.
evaluations.baseline: Earlier versus later checkpoints of the same U-Net and the unrescaled curves for each dataset size

evaluations.setting: Same CelebA U-Nets with n from 512 to 32768, evaluated at diffusion time t=0.01
evaluations.metric: Empirical denoising train loss and held-out test loss
evaluations.result: Train and test losses initially coincide and later separate; separation approximately aligns after rescaling by tau/n. At n=32768 the gap remains small even after 11M updates.
evaluations.baseline: Training loss versus held-out test loss and raw-time versus n-rescaled plots

evaluations.setting: Full-batch CelebA training for n in [128,512]
evaluations.metric: FID and normalized f_mem versus tau/n
evaluations.result: Memorization onset remains delayed approximately linearly with n even though every sample is included in every update.
evaluations.baseline: Fixed-min(512,n) minibatch experiments and the equal-exposure hypothesis

evaluations.setting: CelebA U-Nets with W in {8,16,32,48,64}, corresponding to approximately 0.26M-16M trainable parameters
evaluations.metric: FID and normalized f_mem curve collapse; empirical (n,p) no-copy boundaries
evaluations.result: Curves approximately support tau_gen proportional to W^-1 and tau_mem proportional to n/W; no-copy boundaries rise with longer stopping times.
evaluations.baseline: Raw checkpoint time and smaller-width networks

evaluations.setting: CelebA U-Net with W=64 trained by Adam at learning rate 1e-4
evaluations.result: The two stages and approximate n-scaled memorization onset persist but occur in fewer optimizer steps than with SGD momentum.
evaluations.baseline: SGD with momentum at learning rate 0.01

evaluations.setting: d=8 balanced two-Gaussian mixture with a residual MLP score, full-batch SGD, n=256-4096 and W=64-256
evaluations.metric: Estimated KL divergence D_KL(P_theta || P_0) and f_mem
evaluations.result: KL first approaches zero and later increases with copying; the late transition approximately collapses under tau/n and tau W, while tau_gen versus W is inconclusive.
evaluations.baseline: Known analytic population score and unrescaled training curves

evaluations.setting: Classifier-free conditional generation on the same two-component Gaussian mixture, W=64, n in {256,512,1024}
evaluations.result: The three displayed memorization curves approximately collapse under n rescaling.

evaluations.setting: Random-feature score matching on Gaussian data at fixed t with d=100, psi_p=64, and varying psi_n
evaluations.metric: Train/test denoising loss, true-score error, and predicted tau_mem-rescaled time
evaluations.result: Loss separation and score degradation align after the predicted slow-time rescaling; generalization loss heatmaps move with the stopping time.
evaluations.baseline: Closed-form gradient-flow prediction and infinite-time learning curves from prior random-feature analysis

evaluations.setting: Finite random-feature matrices with isotropic and two-point covariance spectra
evaluations.metric: Empirical eigenvalue histograms versus Theorem 3.1 Stieltjes-density solutions
evaluations.result: At d=100 the plots show a small finite-sample bulk, a larger population-covariance bulk, and an atom near the predicted locations.
evaluations.baseline: Numerical solution of the asymptotic spectral equations

evaluations.setting: Random-feature robustness checks across diffusion time, non-unit data variance, and Adam
evaluations.metric: Train/test-loss curve collapse and score-error scaling
evaluations.result: Predicted slow-time rescaling remains qualitatively consistent; minimum score error is fitted as approximately 0.20 psi_n^-0.59, and Adam retains an n-scaled onset.
evaluations.baseline: Unit-variance, t=0.1, full-batch gradient-descent reference setting

limitations: Author-stated: practical diffusion training usually uses Adam; only one Adam configuration is checked, and optimizer-dependent absolute times remain open.
Author-stated: the main image experiments are unconditional; conditional evidence is limited to a toy Gaussian mixture.
Author-stated: U-Net capacity spans only roughly 1M-16M parameters in the main sweep, so the full proposed (n,p) phase diagram is unmapped.
Author-stated: the theory uses controlled data and frozen random features rather than structured learned architectures or rich image distributions.
Reviewer-identified: the natural-image study uses only downsampled grayscale CelebA and reports no independent training seeds per configuration.
Reviewer-identified: confidence intervals resample test sets, noise, or generated samples, not optimizer trajectories, and no confidence interval is reported for the n exponent.
Reviewer-identified: FID and the hard L2 nearest-neighbor ratio can miss partial, transformed, or semantic memorization and do not measure privacy extraction risk.
Reviewer-identified: checkpoint steps are not compute-matched across width, batch size, or optimizer.
Reviewer-identified: the architectural infinite-time threshold is extrapolated from a finite 2M-update plateau.
Reviewer-identified: the random-feature theory trains at one fixed diffusion time and does not analyze the coupled all-time score network used for generation.
Reviewer-identified: the general-covariance Gaussian-equivalence/replica derivation is acknowledged as heuristic in places despite a separate claim of rigor.
Reviewer-identified: the meaning of p changes from total trainable U-Net parameters to random-feature count, while the learned random-feature layer actually has dp entries.
Reviewer-identified: the score-error exponent -0.59 is a numerical fit, and a full diffusion KL conclusion would require score accuracy integrated over all noise times.
Reviewer-identified: no flow-matching or stochastic-interpolant experiment supports the conclusion's cross-family extrapolation.
failure_modes: If a deployment trains beyond the data- and optimizer-specific tau_mem, early dynamical regularization disappears and close replicas can emerge.
If tau_mem is selected from a different dataset, resolution, conditioning scheme, augmentation policy, optimizer, or architecture, the empirical n/W rule may not transfer.
If memorization is semantic or localized rather than an almost exact pixel-space replica, the f_mem monitor may remain near zero while privacy leakage persists.
FID may stay flat or improve while copying increases, so sample quality alone is not a safe stopping rule.
At low n or sufficiently high effective capacity, tau_mem can approach tau_gen and eliminate the useful stopping window.
At very large n relative to the feature class, architectural underfitting may prevent memorization but also cap generation quality.
Adaptive optimizers or learning-rate schedules can compress or shift both timescales, invalidating a rule expressed only in update count.
Heavy-tailed or strongly non-Gaussian data can violate the random-feature covariance assumptions and alter spectral edges.
Learned features and attention can create evolving spectra that a frozen random-feature two-bulk model does not capture.
A finite apparent no-copy plateau can be mistaken for an infinite-time architectural phase when memorization is merely later than the training budget.
Conditional classes with unequal support can enter generalization and memorization at different times, defeating one global checkpoint.
A stopping rule calibrated on one training realization may be unstable when run-to-run variance is material.
reusable_insights: Separate useful generalization time from overfit or extraction time instead of treating convergence as one event.
Plot originality metrics alongside quality metrics because FID can improve while exact-copy behavior worsens.
Use full-batch or exposure-matched controls before attributing a dataset-size time law to simple sample repetition.
When width is the intervention, report the implied law in both width and actual parameter/FLOP units.
A split empirical spectrum can turn optimization into a multiscale filter: early stopping retains fast population modes and suppresses slow sample-specific modes.
Audit source revision and public submission dates because a nearly identical concurrent result can sharply narrow novelty.
Distinguish finite-budget no-copy contours from a true infinite-time capacity threshold.
Estimate stopping-time uncertainty across independent training runs, not only by resampling evaluation examples.
Test copying thresholds against transformed and semantic-neighbor metrics before making privacy claims.
open_questions: Does tau_mem remain linear in n for modern latent, text-conditioned, high-resolution diffusion and flow-matching models under compute-matched training?
What invariant time coordinate, such as examples processed, gradient-flow time, optimizer preconditioned path length, or FLOPs, transfers across optimizers and widths?
Can tau_gen and tau_mem be estimated online with preregistered thresholds and confidence intervals rather than retrospectively from plots?
How much independent-run variance is present in the claimed n and W exponents?
Do semantic, partial, and membership-inference measures enter memorization on the same timescale as the pixel-neighbor ratio?
Can an all-diffusion-time learned-feature theory derive the two bulks without frozen random features?
What conditions make the general-covariance Gaussian-equivalence result rigorous, and do heavy-tailed data change the slow spectral edge?
How does class conditioning split tau_gen and tau_mem across rare and common conditions?
Is the apparent U-Net architectural threshold stable under training far beyond two million updates?
Can the overlapping claims with arXiv:2505.16959v2 be experimentally separated by a head-to-head protocol covering the same datasets and metrics?

competitive_landscape.title: Bigger Isn't Always Memorizing: Early Stopping Overparameterized Diffusion Models
competitive_landscape.difference: Favero, Sclocchi, and Wyart were publicly submitted one day earlier and independently report the same core law tau_mem proportional to dataset size, the competition between generalization and memorization times, early-stopping guidance, and a phase diagram across image and language diffusion. The present paper adds a random-feature two-bulk spectral analysis, U-Net width scaling, full-batch and Adam controls, and Gaussian-mixture checks, so the dataset-linear headline is not uniquely novel.

competitive_landscape.title: Denoising Score Matching with Random Features: Insights on Diffusion Models from Precise Learning Curves
competitive_landscape.difference: George, Veiga, and Macris derive asymptotically precise train/test learning curves and generalization-memorization regimes for random-feature denoising score matching as functions of sample, feature, and noise-sample ratios. The present paper starts from that random-feature setting but resolves finite gradient-flow time and interprets separated spectral bulks as tau_gen and tau_mem.

competitive_landscape.title: Taking a Big Step: Large Learning Rates in Denoising Score Matching Prevent Memorization
competitive_landscape.difference: Wu, Marion, Biau, and Boyer also make irregularity of the small-noise empirical score central, but prove that sufficiently large SGD steps cannot stably approach arbitrarily small excess risk in a one-dimensional two-layer setting. The present paper instead studies finite training duration and slow spectral modes, mostly at a fixed small learning rate, so learning-rate regularization and early stopping are distinct but interacting mechanisms.

competitive_landscape.title: Memorization and Regularization in Generative Diffusion Models
competitive_landscape.difference: Baptista et al. analyze why the empirical score produces memorization in conditioned and unconditioned diffusion and numerically study Tikhonov, consistency, underparameterization, and early-stopping regularizers. The present paper's added claim is the quantitative dataset-linear delay and its random-feature spectral mechanism, not the general proposition that early stopping avoids the empirical minimizer.

competitive_landscape.title: On the Generalization Properties of Diffusion Models
competitive_landscape.difference: Li et al. provide training-dynamics-dependent early-stopping generalization bounds polynomial in dataset size and model capacity, including a mode-shift analysis. The present paper focuses on the onset of sample reproduction, empirical time collapse, and a solvable random-feature spectrum rather than a generalization-gap upper bound.

competitive_landscape.title: Generalization in diffusion models arises from geometry-adaptive harmonic representations
competitive_landscape.difference: Kadkhodaie et al. attribute non-memorizing diffusion to architecture-aligned harmonic shrinkage and show score agreement across disjoint training subsets above a data threshold. The present paper explicitly separates that architectural phase from a finite-time dynamical phase that can exist even when the architecture can eventually memorize.

competitive_landscape.title: An analytic theory of creativity in convolutional diffusion models
competitive_landscape.difference: Kamb and Ganguli explain creativity through locality and equivariance, deriving local-score machines that predict convolutional diffusion outputs. Their mechanism constrains the converged function class; the present paper explains why an expressive class can temporarily approximate population structure before learning dataset-specific detail.

competitive_landscape.title: On Memorization in Diffusion Models
competitive_landscape.difference: Gu et al. define effective model memorization and map how dataset size, distribution, architecture, and training choices affect approximation to the memorizing optimum, including random-label conditioning. The present work concentrates on the temporal onset law and offers spectral dynamics rather than a broad factor survey.

novelty_assessment.author_claim: Training dynamics themselves implicitly regularize overparameterized score models: a dataset-size-independent useful-sampling time precedes a memorization time that grows linearly with n, and two spectral bulks in a random-feature model explain the separation.
novelty_assessment.evidence: CelebA checkpoint sweeps, train/test-loss divergence, full-batch, width, Adam, Gaussian-mixture, conditional, and random-feature spectral experiments all show a qualitatively separated early population-like stage and later sample-specific stage; the supplement derives the linear random-feature flow and asymptotic bulk scales.
novelty_assessment.reviewer_inference: Moderate novelty in the random-feature dynamical spectrum and the unusually broad within-paper triangulation, but low novelty for the headline dataset-linear memorization time and early-stopping window because arXiv:2505.16959v2 independently reports essentially the same central law and was publicly submitted one day earlier. Earlier exact-version work already establishes early-stopping, architecture, and learning-rate regularization. Claims should therefore be narrowed to the two-bulk explanation and the specific width/full-batch/GMM evidence; exact exponent one, infinite-time phase boundaries, general covariance rigor, privacy safety, and transfer to modern conditional or flow models remain unproven.

reviewer_notes: Read arXiv:2505.17638v2 end to end: 40/40 pages, including all 15 figures, the complete reference list, Supplement A-D, Proposition C.1, Theorems 3.1/3.2 and their proofs, Gaussian-equivalence and replica derivations, finite-time bounds, negative/inconclusive width result for tau_gen in the GMM, and optimizer/variance/spectrum appendices. Source identity is pinned to the indexed v2 PDF and extracted text. Competitors were checked on official arXiv exact-version records on 2026-08-23. Author claims, reviewer inferences, and contradiction audits are separated explicitly.
